canberra.title: A Canberra detective spent decades sending crooks to prison. Now he has to join them
canberra.snippet: It was, the police officer admitted, “the dumbest thing I’ve ever done”. Detective Leading Senior Constable Trent Madde...
canberra.content:
21 August 2026

Detective Trent Madders leaves court after pleading guilty earlier this year. Photo: Albert McKnight.

It was, the police officer admitted, “the dumbest thing I’ve ever done”.

Detective Leading Senior Constable Trent Madders was speaking about how he repeatedly lied to the ACT Magistrates Court during the prosecution of two brothers he had been investigating.

But despite his regrets, these lies eventually led to his being sent to the same place as those he tried to protect the community from during his nearly 25 years in the police force.

On Friday (21 August), the 52-year-old faced the ACT Supreme Court and was sentenced to about 11 months’ jail, suspended after he spent four months behind bars.

“Overall, the conduct reflects a tragic misjudgement on the part of a police officer,” Justice David Mossop said.

Court documents show Madders led an investigation into a man in 2019. Officers then raided the man’s home and seized his laptop as well as his brother’s mobile phone.

Although the laptop and phone were legally required to be forensically examined within 30 days, this was not done.

The day after this 30-day period ended, a digital forensics team member emailed Madders to say the team was processing the devices. Both devices were found to contain material that was relevant to the investigation.

Meanwhile, both the man and his brother pleaded not guilty and the matter went to a hearing in the ACT Magistrates Court in 2020, during which Madders gave evidence.

When cross-examined about whether he knew the phone and laptop had been examined outside the 30-day period, he repeatedly claimed two digital forensics team members assured him the examination took place within that window.

But when the two digital forensic team members gave evidence, they said they had never told him this.

Justice Mossop said Madders’ statements were knowingly, rather than recklessly, false.

The judge said he made these statements while a serving police officer in charge of the investigation, repeated them multiple times and continued to do so despite opportunities for reflection.

“The conduct which the perjury intended to hide was a procedural breach of the law,” Justice Mossop said.

He said Madders served in the Air Force from 1992 and then joined the Australian Federal Police (AFP) in 2000. He was suspended due to this offence and will likely be fired from his job.

Justice Mossop said Madders dedicated his professional life to serving the public, noting that serving in the police force had come at a considerable personal cost.

He had no prior criminal history, was remorseful and had been assessed as having a low likelihood of reoffending.

But Justice Mossop said police officers lying in their evidence during court hearings was “conduct that strikes at the heart of criminal justice”.

It also affected the perception of police officers’ honesty and reliability in general, he said.

After Madders is released from custody in December 2026, he must complete a 12-month good behaviour order.

canberra.title: ACT Policing warn of potentially deadly drugs after five suspected overdose deaths in two weeks
canberra.snippet: ACT Policing has issued a public warning about potentially lethal illicit drugs circulating in Canberra after five suspected fatal overdo...
canberra.content:
21 August 2026

Start the conversation

ACT Policing, ACT Ambulance Service and Directions Health Services warned the community about the dangers of potentially lethal illicit drugs following five suspected overdose deaths in the ACT over the past fortnight. Photo: Naziya Alvi.

ACT Policing has issued a public warning about potentially lethal illicit drugs circulating in Canberra after five suspected fatal overdoses and two non-fatal overdoses were recorded in the past fortnight.

While the exact causes of the deaths are yet to be determined by the Coroner, police suspect opioids were involved in all five cases.

Detective Superintendent Peta Lankester said the cluster of suspected overdoses had prompted police to alert the community to the risks associated with illicit drugs.

“Whilst the exact causes of those overdoses are yet to be determined, we actually suspect that opioids are involved in all cases,” she said.

Police said each death involved a different individual and investigations into every case remain ongoing before findings are referred to the Coroner.

Asked whether the deaths were linked to a contaminated batch of drugs, Detective Superintendent Lankester said police could not draw that conclusion.

Instead, she said the recent deaths reinforced the dangers associated with illicit substances.

“Police would like to issue a warning about illicit drugs in the ACT that can have this impact and harm to the community,” she said.

She urged people to seek immediate medical help if they suspected someone had overdosed.

“Our message to drug users and those around them is to be aware of the signs of an overdose and to seek medical assistance at your earliest opportunity.”

Warning signs of overdoses can include drowsiness, loss of consciousness, unusual breathing and skin turning blue or grey.

ACT Ambulance Service said paramedics had not experienced an overall increase in workload despite the recent overdoses, but stressed that anyone showing signs of an overdose should receive emergency assistance immediately.

“If you are concerned that they are suffering symptoms of an overdose and are deteriorating, please don’t hesitate to call us,” paramedic Sam Perillo said.

Health organisations are also encouraging people who use illicit or unregulated drugs to access Canberra’s drug-checking service, CanTEST.

Directions Health Services chief executive officer Bronwyn Hendry said recent testing had detected substances people were not expecting to find.

“We found heroin in cocaine a couple of times recently, so people have really thought they’re just taking what they think is a relatively mild party drug and have had some serious consequences associated with that,” she said.

She said CanTEST had also identified nitazenes – highly potent synthetic opioids – in drugs sold as heroin and, in some cases, stimulant drugs.

Ms Hendry encouraged people to have drugs tested before use and to carry naloxone, a medication that temporarily reverses opioid overdoses.

“It’s just such a simple thing to administer … that can reverse an overdose and save someone’s life, but you do need to call the ambulance as well,” she said.

Naloxone is available for free from CanTEST, CAHMA, the Civic and Woden Needle and Syringe Programs and some pharmacies.

She also warned people not to assume medicines purchased online were genuine.

According to Directions Health Services, some drugs sold as prescription opioids or benzodiazepines have been found to contain different or more potent substances than expected.

Detective Superintendent Lankester said every suspected overdose death was one too many.

canberra.title: ‘Tom, you are a hero’: Family of tragic Dunlop house fire thank the man who saved them
canberra.snippet: A woman whose family home was destroyed by fire in Dunlop on Wednesday morning recalled the chilling experience of being woken and evacua...
canberra.content:
The family whose home was devastated by a house fire in Dunlop has thanked the man who woke them up and helped them evacuate. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

A woman whose family home was destroyed by fire in Dunlop on Wednesday morning recalled the chilling experience of being woken and evacuated by her hero neighbour.

Kayla Dixon and her family were asleep on Wednesday morning (19 August) when their garage caught alight and flames began to tear through the house.

Their neighbour Tom Freeman was on his way to work when he noticed the smoke, before breaking down their door and evacuating Kayla, her partner and her 14-year-old daughter.

As Kayla and her family begin to rebuild what was lost during the fire, she has thanked Tom publicly, stating that his act of bravery saved her family’s life.

“We are devastated, but we are here. And we are only here because of our incredible neighbour, Tom,” she said.

“Tom, you are a hero. You woke us up, you alerted the neighbourhood and you saved our lives. We will never be able to thank you enough.”

Kippax Butcher Tom Freeman saved a Dunlop family from a house fire on Wednesday morning by breaking down the front door and waking up the unsuspecting residents inside. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

Kayla and her partner moved into their Dunlop home earlier this year.

A few months later, Kayla’s daughter, who had been living in Western Australia, moved back to Canberra and into their new family home. A week later, Kayla learnt she was pregnant with her second child.

Four months later, their home was destroyed by what was believed to be a couple of electric scooters catching alight.

Kayla’s cat Marshal sadly didn’t survive the fire. Photo: Kayla Dixon.

With the home destroyed, the biggest loss was that of their cat, Marshal. Kayla said Marshal was as close to a child as a pet could be, having been by her side for more than seven years.

“Marshal wasn’t just a pet to me. He was my son. He was a seven-year-old soulmate who gave me the strength to survive my absolute worst times,” she said.

“The past year, after I finished working at Aussies Cafe in Parliament House, I went through a previous severe domestic violence and a toxic friendship. This left me alone, jobless and homeless, living out of my car. I had nothing and no-one – except for my cat, Marshal.

“Marshal is the reason my partner and I stayed together; when I had to figure out housing, my partner volunteered to look after Marshal so he would be safe.

“[Eventually] a mate called out of the blue and offered me a caretaking role looking after a home in Dunlop.

“I jumped at it because it meant I could stay in Canberra and finally have a real roof over our heads. When I went to get Marshal, I didn’t just bring him back, I brought my partner home with us too.”

When initially evacuating, Kayla’s partner picked up Marshal and brought him outside. Tragically, in a state of confusion, Marshal attacked him and ran back into the building. Emergency services later found his body inside.

Despite having everything stripped away in one moment, Kayla and her family are thankful to the Dunlop community for its support.

“We also want to send our deepest gratitude to every single emergency department and first responder involved,” she said.

“The fire crews who looked after us when our entire world fell apart in front of our eyes. Thank you.

“To Canberra Busways for helping us travel. To my daughter’s best friend and her mum for giving us a safe place to stay. And to my daughter’s friends for supporting her. We are so grateful to you all.

“Thank you, Dunlop and surrounding suburbs, for listening to our story. Please hug your family and your pets a little tighter tonight. You never know when it’s the last time.”

A GoFundMe page has been set up to support Kayla and her family as they begin to rebuild. To donate, visit the page here.

canberra.title: Guilty pleas entered over Kings Highway crash that killed man, critically injured woman
canberra.snippet: Joyce Catherine Wilkie has pleaded guilty to two driving charges over a Kings Highway crash that killed one man and critically injured hi...
canberra.content:
21 August 2026

Terrence O’Dwyer was killed, and Shirlee Donai critically injured, in the 2024 crash on the Kings Highway outside of Braidwood. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Joyce Catherine Wilkie has pleaded guilty to two driving charges over a Kings Highway crash that killed one man and critically injured his partner.

The now-74-year-old pleaded guilty to one count of negligent driving (occasioning death) and one count of negligent driving (occasioning grievous bodily harm) as she fronted Queanbeyan Local Court earlier this month.

Sixty-seven-year-old Terrence O’Dwyer was killed in the crash, and his partner Shirlee Donai, then 68, was left with severe injuries.

The agreed statement of facts outlined that on 7 November 2024, Wilkie left Moruya between 2 and 3 pm to head towards her farm in Gundaroo.

She stopped at Batemans Bay for fish and chips, plus some ice-cream, at about 3:30 pm, before she kept driving.

That’s the last memory she has before the crash.

“The offender indicated her next memory is ‘waking up in a room in Canberra Hospital and being told that I had been in a motor vehicle accident,'” the court documents showed.

Ms Donai was driving a Toyota Aurion sedan with Mr O’Dwyer in the passenger seat. They’d been to a medical appointment in Goulburn and were driving to Braidwood on the Kings Highway.

At the same time, Wilkie was also on the Kings Highway in her Volkswagen Transporter utility.

About 1.3 km after the Mayfield Road turnoff (near the Warri area), at some point between 5:30 pm and 5:35 pm, Wilkie “failed to negotiate a left-hand bend, crossing the unbroken centre lines and into the oncoming eastbound lane”, court documents showed.

Her ute “briefly glanced” the safety barrier before she kept driving on the wrong side of the road.

That’s when the two vehicles collided.

“The passenger side of the offender’s vehicle heavily impacted the victim’s oncoming Toyota,” the documents showed.

Mr O’Dwyer suffered head injuries and was declared dead at the scene. Ms Donai was taken to Canberra Hospital in a critical condition.

She experienced multiple rib fractures, bruising, chest pain and hypoxia.

It was a clear, dry day and no defects were found with Wilkie’s vehicle that could have contributed to the crash.

No alcohol or drugs were found in her system, and records showed she wasn’t using her phone when she crossed onto the wrong side of the highway.

Wilkie was also originally charged with dangerous driving occasioning death and causing bodily harm by willful neglect while in charge of a motor vehicle, but these charges have since been dismissed.

She’s due to next appear in court on 8 December.

Original Article published by Claire Fenwicke on About Regional.

canberra.title: PM calls for independent investigation into aid workers’ deaths after ‘outrageous’ Israeli findings
canberra.snippet: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has called for an independent investigation into a drone missile attack on a World Central Kitchen convoy...
canberra.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has called for an independent investigation into the killings of seven aid workers in Gaza. Photo: Thomas Lucraft.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has called for an independent investigation into a drone missile attack on a World Central Kitchen convoy and the deaths of seven aid workers including Australian Zomi Frankcom in Gaza in April 2024, after the Israeli military cleared itself of any wrongdoing on Wednesday (19 August).

Speaking on the ABC’s 7.30 on Thursday night, Mr Albanese echoed Senator Penny Wong’s comments earlier in the day when she described the findings as an “outrage”, and added that he thought an independent investigation should be considered.

“It clearly is an outrage, and there’s a need for a far more transparent and clear explanation from the Israeli Government other than what we’ve received,” he said.

“I would’ve thought [an independent investigation] is one of the options that certainly should be considered.

“But it’s certainly not good enough that on World Humanitarian Day of all days, they release this so-called report that essentially says, ‘Yes, we’re responsible, but nothing to see here’.

“We will press the Israeli Government,” he added.

“The direction, we have said today, we’ll discuss with Ms Frankcom’s family. They deserve to be consulted on these issues, and we’ll do that, and then we’ll make an announcement in the coming days.”

The PM’s comments came after Israel’s Ambassador to Australia Hillel Newman was summoned by Senator Wong to explain the outcomes of the Israel Defense Force’s (IDF) investigation.

After the meeting, Mr Newman defended the investigation, saying, “One cannot attack the findings of a court if the findings are not suitable to one’s political agenda”.

Asked whether Israel would apologise to the family of Ms Frankcom, Mr Newman said while he expressed sorrow to the family for her death, to issue an apology may have “legal ramifications”.

“Israel came out with findings after a thorough investigation, after a two-year investigation into the circumstances of the death of Zomi Frankcom,” he said.

“Since I took up my mission here about five months ago, I was implored all the time to bring about closure, which I did.

“But in the end, one must also understand that not every case where someone dies, where there is a casualty, that that means there is a criminal liability.”

Mr Newman echoed the investigation’s findings by saying the World Central Kitchen group had used armed security to protect the three vehicles in which the aid workers were travelling, and that the convoy had not taken the route which the IDF hadn’t approved.

“It was a mistake in retrospect, but the findings of the court are there was no criminal intention … and therefore there was no criminal responsibility.”

After the meeting, Senator Wong said the explanation was unsatisfactory, that the outcome had fallen short of the accountability the Australian Government expected of Israel, and said that many questions remained unanswered.

“We do not have confidence in the IDF military Advocate General’s process given the many unanswered questions,” she said.

“The Australian Government does not believe the removal of two officers from their positions and three officers being reprimanded is sufficient accountability for the deaths of seven people including an Australian citizen,” she told media, referring to the actions of the IDF in the days immediately after the attack.

She also referred to Australia’s recent relationship with Israel as “difficult”.

“Obviously it’s a difficult time in our relationship. We made our views clear about this issue,” she said.

In a statement, Ms Frankcom’s brother said the family was “deeply disappointed by the decision by Israel’s Military Advocate General to clear their soldiers of criminal wrongdoing in the Gaza strike that killed our beloved Zomi”, adding that the announcement of the findings on World Humanitarian day was an extra “insult to my sister’s memory”.

“We and the families of the six other World Central Kitchen aid workers have been waiting for justice for over two years, hoping and calling for an independent criminal investigation,” he said.

“Zomi and her colleagues deserve more than an internal, opaque process that ends with a short statement by the Israeli Military absolving their soldiers of criminal wrongdoing.

“The families of the victims deserve transparency and an independent judicial assessment of the criminal responsibility for the international humanitarian law violations that took place on that day.”

Greens Senator Mahreen Faruqi said she was “angry and devasted” by the investigation’s findings, but added, “there are no surprises here”.

“This is how the apartheid, genocidal state of Israel works,” she said. “This is a state that routinely commits war crimes with no consequences.

“Zomi and six of her colleagues were systematically hunted and murdered by the Israel Army. This was without a doubt a war crime.”

Senator Faruqi also called for the expulsion of Ambassador Newman, and said the Australian Government had failed Ms Frankcom.

“Israel was never going to hold their forces to account for the murder of Zomi Frankcom,” she added.

“Senator Wong can be as outraged as she wants now, but words don’t cut it. In her meeting with the Israeli Ambassador, she should be telling him to pack his bags and expel him.”

Original Article published by Andrew McLaughlin on PS News.

australia.title: Australia news live: Hiker Lily Hooper remembered as someone ‘everyone liked’; testing under way after dozens of little penguins found dead
australia.snippet: Follow today’s news live Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Woman behind allegation of sexual assault linked to...
australia.content:
Tributes flow for hiker Lily Hooper

Kat Wong

Lily Hooper has been remembered for her smile, her talent and her toughness as the local community reels in the wake of the teenage hiker’s death.

The 18-year-old’s body was recovered from the dense bush of the NSW Southern Highlands overnight, eight days after she was reported missing and the night after it was incorrectly communicated that she had been found alive.

Condolences have poured in for her family and her martial arts teacher, Mark Szalajko, paid tribute to Hooper in a post on social media.

She was a talented and tough martial artist, but despite that toughness, Lily was such a lovely person. She was one of those people who everyone simply liked.

As a martial arts teacher, people walk into and out of our lives every day for many different reasons. Some leave a positive impact on us and on our dojo, and we wish they could have stayed longer. Lily was one of those people.

I will really miss her smile, her conversations and the moments we shared on the mat.

The Wollondilly Performing Arts centre and Wollondilly Shire library have been lit up in purple in memory of Hooper and on Friday evening, a vigil will be held in Oakdale, where she lived with her family.

Guardian reporter Ima Caldwell visited the now-still command post last night – read more below.

What we learned, Friday 21 August

That’s where we’ll leave our live coverage for the day.

Before we let you go, let’s look at the day’s top headlines:

  • Anthony Albanese has said he should not have appeared on a podcast where he engaged in a joke about the Japanese prime minister’s gift to him of melons.

  • Purchases of Australian property by overseas investors have plunged since the government announced an extension of a ban on foreigners buying Australian homes.

  • The body of missing bushwalker Lily Hooper has been recovered from NSW southern highlands overnight, NSW police confirmed. Friends and family of the 18-year-old have paid tribute.

  • The foreign minister, Penny Wong, phoned her Israeli counterpart overnight to discuss the decision not to pursue a criminal investigation into drone strikes in Gaza that killed Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom and six of her colleagues.

  • Dean Cox, the coach of the Sydney Swans, acknowledged the culture of the Swans “has taken a hit”.

  • The Plymouth Brethren Christian church has denied it secretly paid far-right influencers to stage stunts targeting Anthony Albanese and other politicians.

  • The chief executive of Catholic Schools NSW, Dallas McInerney, has been sacked from his position after his appearance at the NSW Icac’s inquiry into allegations of corruption in the state’s Liberal party.

  • The AFP have arrested a dual Russian-Australian citizen who has been charged with attempting to intentionally engage in foreign interference.

  • The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) is investigating a “potential traffic conflict” after two Qantas aircraft came close to colliding while taxiing at Sydney Airport on Tuesday. It is the airport’s fourth safety incident in less than a month.

  • A further 23 dead little penguins have been found on Tasmania’s King Island with tests under way to determine whether the birds died from H5 bird flu.

Thanks for sticking around, have a lovely weekend!

Penry Buckley

Following from the previous post: the parliamentary committee voted 4-3 to find the director of public prosecutions, Sally Dowling, had given false evidence about the pitching of the story to 2GB. But the NSW attorney general, Michael Daley, and the DPP rejected the findings.

The government commissioned a review by former NSW bar association president Noel Hutley which said there was no “no positive basis” to reject Dowling’s account “and find that she, in fact, gave false evidence”.

The committee described difficulty hearing from key DPP witnesses from a meeting about pitching the story to appear before the inquiry, after a court decision last year in favour of the Minns government which means that parliament can no longer compel witnesses.

The Australian high court will hear an appeal in that case later this year.

Penry Buckley

NSW judge cannot hear three criminal cases amid dispute with state’s top prosecutor, court rules

A NSW judge at the centre of a dispute which saw a parliamentary committee find the state’s top prosecutor gave false evidence under oath cannot hear three criminal cases after declining to recuse herself, a court has ruled.

A decision by the NSW court of criminal appeal today ruled the cases be heard by a judge other than district court judge Penelope Wass, finding she has a “long-standing grievance, or series of grievances”, against the Director of Public Prosecutions, Sally Dowling, and that she was “wrong … in declining to disqualify herself” from the proceedings.

It comes after Wass made a written submission to a parliamentary inquiry examining protections against identifying children in court proceedings.

She alleged Dowling personally authorised her department to share details to radio station 2GB of a sentencing hearing in which Wass allowed an Indigenous child to perform an acknowledgement of country.

Wass is among district court judges who have criticised the handling of sexual assault prosecutions under Dowling. Dowling denied she was responsible for pitching the story, alleging Wass had a “personal grievance” against her and her department.

Following Wass’s submission, the DPP asked her to recuse herself from four criminal proceedings on the basis of apprehended bias. She agreed to recuse herself from one, but declined to recuse herself from three others, including a judge-alone child sexual abuse trial.

Monique Ryan says Sydney Swans incident highlights ‘significant cultural issues’ in the sport

Independent MP Monique Ryan says this week’s Sydney Swans incident has highlighted a number of broader issues within the AFL and has called for greater efforts to address them.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Ryan said:

There does appear to be significant cultural issues within the AFL. It was not just this incident, we also have the close relationship with the gambling industry, allegations of racism from AFL players, AFLW players, and also appearing to fail to support players with CTE and concussion.

They need to take action in all those areas in the next year or two to bring back the social licence and respect for the institution that so many Victorians have.

Cait Kelly

Social services council calls on government to protect people amid rising unemployment

The Australian Council of Social Service has called on the government to lift income support, reform employment services and tackle inflation as the unemployment rate rose to 4.5% this week.

ACOSS’s CEO, Cassandra Goldie:

There are already over 100,000 more people unemployed than four years ago when interest rates started to rise, and the RBA expects unemployment to rise to 4.8% by 2028 – that’s another 50,000 people out of paid work.

There are better ways to curb inflation than sacrificing more people to unemployment. The people most affected by rising unemployment and inflation are those living on the lowest incomes in our community, receiving poverty-level income support payments like jobseeker. These are people who were offered no additional financial support in the federal budget.

The government must act urgently to make sure people are protected and we are well-prepared for any potential economic downturn.

Huge cocaine bust sparked by drugs floating in water

Two men have been charged as part of an ongoing probe into Australia’s largest cocaine seizure, AAP reports.

Brisbane man Richard Huynh, 41, has been arrested after being accused of facilitating the shipment of almost three tonnes of cocaine from Queensland to NSW and Victoria through a transport business.

A 23-year-old Sydney man has been also been accused of being part of a criminal syndicate after allegedly being found with a semi-automatic 9mm pistol and a loaded sawn-off shotgun along with ammunition and a silencer.

Huynh was charged after a Kangaroo Point home was searched and $80,000 in cash and electronic devices was seized. Several electronic devices were also seized for digital forensic analysis, police said.

Huynh was arrested at Brisbane airport on Thursday and charged with a number of offences. His matter was listed for Brisbane’s magistrates court today; he did not apply for bail and the case was adjourned to 18 September.

The Sydney man was charged on Thursday after an Erskine Park, NSW residence was searched. Officers seized the guns, ammunition and silencer along with about 28g of cocaine and about $10,000 in cash in suspected proceeds of crime.

He has been charged with a number of firearms and drug offences and appeared in Penrith local court on Thursday.

Petra Stock

SA government releases official ‘incredibly concerning’ cuttlefish counts

South Australia’s environment minister, Emily Bourke, said giant cuttlefish numbers in the state’s upper Spencer gulf were “significantly low and incredibly concerning”.

This year’s population estimate suggested there were 1,811 giant Australian cuttlefish off the coast of Whyalla this year – a record low since counts began in 1998 and down from about 63,000 in 2025.

Zero cuttlefish were observed during the standard cuttlefish surveys conducted by the SA Research and Development Institute (Sardi) in June and July, which the institute called an “unprecedented decrease”. But a modified method, and more extensive surveys by the environment department, which included searching for cuttlefish under rocks with torches, estimated there were 1,811 animals.

Prof Mike Steer, the Sardi executive director, said the harmful algal bloom, which reached the cuttlefish breeding area over Summer, was the likely cause for the low numbers. He said:

Cuttlefish breed one year, die and then the resulting hatchlings will make up the population next year. So next year’s survey is going to be really important.

Read more here:

More dead little penguins found on King Island with bird flu testing under way

Lisa Cox

A further 23 dead little penguins have been found on Tasmania’s King Island with tests under way to determine whether the birds died from H5 bird flu.

It follows the detection of 28 dead little penguins on the island on Wednesday, with test results from those birds also still pending. The state has not indicated at this stage that it suspects bird flu.

Other birds on the island have been confirmed positive for the deadly strain.

The state’s natural resources and environment department said this included four silver gulls, two crested terns, and one white-fronted tern collected at beaches and bays near the island’s main township of Currie. Of the 18 confirmed H5 bird flu cases in Tasmania so far, 14 were found around Currie.

Incident controller Wes Ford said the government was “deploying more staff to increase our surveillance, monitoring and collection activities in the area”:

We are committed to supporting the King Island community and local industries through ongoing surveillance, regular communication and timely advice as we continue to monitor the situation.

Deakin University’s Prof Euan Ritchie said with bird flu a possible cause of the penguin deaths, the state needed to mobilise all resources it could to protect the island’s wildlife, which included threatened species that had declined to very low numbers such as the King Island scrubtit and brown thornbill:

If bird flu were to affect these species it would be a disaster.

The developments follow a “significant escalation” in H5 bird flu in South Australia after the discovery of three mass mortality events involving more than 1,000 greater crested terns.

David Pocock on the ‘real betrayal’ of Labor’s deal on gambling reforms – Australian Politics podcast

This week, the Albanese government passed major reforms to online gambling advertising and deep cuts to rein in NDIS spending – all with the Coalition’s support.

David Pocock has long been a vocal critic of the government’s approach to both of these issues. He argues Labor and the opposition have failed to stand up to vested interests on gambling reforms. And while he agrees NDIS cuts are needed, he says major parties have ignored expert evidence on the value of community participation and are handing over important decisions to algorithms with little scrutiny.

Political editor Tom McIlroy speaks to the independent senator about what he thinks this notable week of deal-making means for the nation’s political future – while both major parties continue to be spooked by One Nation’s rise.

Listen here:

Nick Visser

That’s all from me. Achol Arok is here to guide you into the weekend. Take care.

Thousands of little penguins being vaccinated against H5 bird flu in Victoria

Victoria has begun vaccinating about 5,000 little penguins at Phillip Island and St Kilda to protect them against the deadly H5 bird flu, in what is believed to be the world’s largest vaccination program involving wild birds.

While vaccinating wild birds against the disease was challenging, the fact that the penguins returned home every night to Phillip Island and St Kilda made it possible to deliver the two doses necessary over a two-week period.

Sarah Basford Canales

Tony Abbott’s role advising rightwing group ‘very informal’

The former prime minister, Tony Abbott, provided an “exchange of ideas in a very informal way” while an advisory board member for rightwing activist group, Advance.

The third-party group is appearing before a parliamentary inquiry this afternoon where its chair, Vicki Dunne, was asked about the nature of Abbott’s role with the group.

Ahead of being elected the Liberal party’s federal president, Guardian Australia reported Abbott was stepping down from his role advising the group.

Dunne, a former Liberal ACT assembly member for 19 years, explained:

He was on an … advisory board, and that’s, that was generally, you know, ‘hey, what do you think about this idea?’ and or, and vice versa … it was an exchange of ideas in a very informal way.

Dunne said she couldn’t remember who else sat on the advisory board.

[The advisory board] was more prominent when Advance was setting up, and it’s become – as the board has matured and the organisation has matured – I think that there’s less [of a] role for an advisory, a sort of a non-formal advisory committee.

AFP details foreign interference charge against dual Russia-Australian citizen

The AFP commissioner, Krissy Barrett, is holding a press conference after the agency said earlier today a 27-year-old man had been charged with foreign interference.

The man, a dual Australian and Russian citizen, is a resident of Victoria and was arrested in Brisbane yesterday with multiple devices seized.

He is charged with attempting to engage in intentional foreign interference, which carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison. Barrett said:

We will allege the 27-year-old man sought to provide information about Ukrainian military activities to individuals he believed were linked to Russian intelligence services.

She went on to say the man is alleged to have travelled to Russia in October 2024 where he allegedly undertook “military-style training” before returning to Australia in December 2024. Barrett said he is then alleged to have travelled to Ukraine in May 2025, where he joined the Ukrainian armed forces and gained access to information about Ukrainian military operations and personnel.

He then allegedly provided or attempted to provide that information to people he believed “were acting on behalf of Russian intelligence”. Barrett said:

It is alleged that this conduct created a risk to the safety and security of Ukrainian military personnel. We allege elements of this offending occurred in Australia and offshore.

Swans AFLW captain says ‘no doubt’ club has taken a ‘reputational hit’ this week

The Swans AFLW captain, Lucy McEvoy, and coach, Colin O’Riordan, spoke a moment ago about the five Sydney Swans players who have been suspended for the rest of the season for breaching club standards.

O’Riordan said:

Growing up, it was taught you treat everyone with respect, and that respect is a fundamental pillar of how you live your life. And that’s especially important in how you treat women. …

The sanctions imposed by the club reflect the seriousness with which this matter is being treated, and as a program, we fully support these sanctions.

McEvoy said the players were “incredibly disappointed” in the matter, although she said “we know the actions of those five players are not a reflection of the broader club”.

We’ve had some really open conversations as a group this week and with the club more broadly. We’ve felt the support both internally and externally … The girls are working through their emotions as they see fit for themselves. Personally, we wrap our arms around everyone as the whole entire club.

There’s no doubt the club has taken a reputational hit this week. And we’ll do whatever we can as a club, in both programs, to make sure we build back the trust and respect of our members and fans and the community more broadly.

australia.title: Australian police charge man accused of attempting to share Ukrainian military intel with Russian agents
australia.snippet: Vladmir Teslov, 27, charged after allegedly seeking to provide information about Ukrainian forces to ‘Russian intelligence services’ Aust...
australia.content:
Australian police have charged a man who allegedly joined the Ukrainian military and sought to provide information about its activities to people he suspected were Russian agents.

Vladimir Teslov, a dual Russian-Australian citizen, appeared in court on Friday after the Australian federal police (AFP) charged him with an attempted foreign interference. The offence carries a 20-year prison sentence.

Police alleged the 27-year-old travelled to Russia to undergo military-style training in October 2024.

When Teslov returned to Australia later that year, he maintained contact “with individuals he believed were connected to Russian intelligence services”, police alleged.

In May last year, he allegedly travelled to Ukraine and joined its armed forces. During this time, he accessed information relating to their military personnel, units and locations, police allege.

The AFP’s commissioner, Krissy Barrett, said an investigation into the man – codenamed Operation Woodcreeper – started in June this year.

It is alleged Teslov’s attempts to share the information “created a risk to the safety and security of Ukrainian military personnel”. He is alleged to have made the attempts in Australia and overseas.

Teslov was arrested on Thursday, with several properties in Brisbane being searched by police, and multiple devices seized.

He was believed to live in Victoria, and was unemployed, police said. There was no suggestion he received military training in Australia, nor worked for any government agency.

Barrett said the investigation was complex, but the man was not suspected to have posed any direct threat to Australia.

There was also no known connection between Teslov and a Russian-born couple, Kira and Igor Korolev, who lived in Brisbane and were charged with espionage offences in 2024, Barrett said. That case is ongoing and the pair have yet to enter a plea.

Barrett did not confirm how long Teslov had lived in Australia. When asked whether he was part of a broader network, she said investigations were continuing and further arrests were possible.

It was also being investigated whether he volunteered his services to the suspected Russian intelligence officials, or was recruited.

Barrett said the AFP had been engaged with domestic and international partners, but “it would be a matter for Ukraine whether they were going to commence any prosecutions”.

It is the eighth time foreign inference charges have been laid in Australia, but the first time the specific offence has involved an alleged offender connected to Russia.

She said Russia, however, had not been targeted by the AFP, despite Australia being an ally of Ukraine.

“Our job is ensuring Australia does not become a safe haven for people who think they can conduct foreign interference on our shores,” Barrett said.

Claire McGuinness, a deputy director-general for the Australian Security and Intelligence Organisation (Asio), said in a statement that foreign interference could represent “both a threat to life and a threat to our way of life.”

“This case should put regimes perpetrating foreign interference on notice: we have zero tolerance,” McGuinness said.

“ASIO’s resolve is firm, and we will continue to work with our close partners to detect and counter attacks on Australia’s sovereignty.

“This achievement demonstrates the rigour, perseverance and agility of Australian agencies. I am immensely proud of ASIO’s outstanding contribution to this case.”

Teslov was refused bail in the Brisbane magistrates court by Magistrate Lewis Shillito on Friday. His matter was adjourned to 2 October.

The Russian embassy in Canberra said it learned of the case as a result of media reports.

“At this stage, no official requests or notifications have been received by the Embassy or the Consulate General in Sydney, either from the Australian authorities or from the individual concerned,” it said in a statement.

“We are currently using the available channels and resources to establish the circumstances of the case.”

australia.content:

The Plymouth Brethren Christian Church has denied it secretly paid far-right influencers to stage stunts targeting Anthony Albanese and other politicians during an appearance at a parliamentary inquiry into the 2025 election.

Volunteers from the Brethren church were seen at polling booths during the campaign, but the religious organisation denied claims it had coordinated hundreds of volunteers to support Liberal candidates across the country.

The family of missing 18-year-old hiker Lily Hooper was told she’d been found alive. “She’s coming home,” her father said – then, their tears of joy turned to grief.

Reporter Ima Caldwell was on the ground in the southern highlands as the final sounds of the search for Hooper faded into the darkness, and “the last traces of light vanished entirely from the sky”.

What they said …

“His head was down. He didn’t look up. I distinctly remember thinking ‘something bad has happened here’.” – a witness in the Alan Jones trial

An alleged victim looked “distraught” while sitting next to Alan Jones, who had his hand under the table, a fellow guest at a lower north shore luncheon has told a Sydney court. The alleged victim, known as complainant C, earlier told the court that Jones had instructed him to sit next to him at the long table and spent the entire lunch with his left hand under the table and either on his leg or on his penis over his pants.

Jones has pleaded not guilty to 20 charges of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching against six complainants.

Political editor Tom McIlroy speaks to independent senator David Pocock about what he thinks the Albanese government’s week of deal-making means for the nation’s political future – with both major parties continuing to be spooked by One Nation’s rise.

On the 40th anniversary of Paul Simon’s pioneering classic Graceland, the author of a new book about the album explains the complex legacy and musicianship of the 1986 masterpiece.

Ethan Beck writes that Graceland remains the most nimble, ecstatic album that Simon’s hands have touched.

australia.title: Former NSW Liberal minister tells Icac ‘cult took over the party’
australia.snippet: David Elliott tells inquiry of branch stacking and death threats as Catholic Schools NSW sack boss after appearance Follow our Australia ...
australia.content:
A former New South Wales Liberal minister has told an inquiry he came to believe “a cult had taken over the party” after branch stacking by the religious right faction, while the chief executive of Catholic Schools NSW has been sacked following his appearance before the corruption watchdog.

Former Liberal minister and MP for the now-abolished seat of Baulkham Hills, David Elliott, told the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption that after he opposed developments by fugitive property developer Jean Nassif, he was followed by private investigators and received death threats.

It came on the same day the chief executive of Catholic Schools NSW, Dallas McInerney, was sacked after appearing at the watchdog’s inquiry into allegations of corruption in the state’s Liberal party.

Icac is investigating the allegation that McInerney arranged and approved illegal political donations that were not declared and exceeded applicable donation caps from Catholic Schools NSW to lobbying companies controlled by the Reformers, to support the recruitment and renewal of members to the Liberal party. The practice, known as branch stacking, is not itself illegal.

Under a separate allegation, Icac is investigating whether Reformer Christian Ellis, and Liberal operatives Jeremy Greenwood and Charles Perrottet took donations from Nassif and his company Toplace in exchange for outcomes including damage to Elliott’s career.

Greenwood has denied payments to lobbying companies controlled by the Reformers were for factional work, while Ellis has moved to the UK and is not expected to give evidence to the inquiry. Charles Perrottet has previously denied any wrongdoing.

On Friday, the inquiry heard how when his seat was abolished by the NSW electoral commission ahead of the March 2023 election, Elliott retired from politics after he was unable to convince local branches to make him their candidate.

Elliott – part of the Liberals’ centre-right faction, which centred at that time around the then prime minister Scott Morrison and the federal MP for Mitchell, Alex Hawke – said branch stacking efforts in the Hills shire “radically” shifted the balance of power, meaning Castle Hill would go to a candidate in the religious right of the party, associated with Dominic Perrottet, and linked to the conservative Catholic organisation, Opus Dei.

“It was all becoming evident to me that … a cult had taken over the Liberal party and particularly that electorate … in the Opus Dei faction, the religious right,” said Elliott.

The inquiry has previously heard legally intercepted phone calls featuring Nassif in which he claimed he had “forced the boys” to get rid of Elliott’s seat of Baulkham Hills, and had sent “Castle Hill fucking hundreds of new members”.

Elliott said that Nassif began to target him after he wrote a letter opposing an ultimately unsuccessful development proposal by Toplace in the northern Sydney suburb of Cherrybrook. “After that letter is when Nassif went nuts,” he told the commission.

Elliott has told Icac he was aware that private investigator Shane de Kauwe was surveying him, referring to him as “the Maxwell Smart of the NSW private investigator industry”. De Kauwe, who is not named in Icac’s allegations, is expected to give evidence to the commission.

Elliott said he began to receive death threats, but he was “not saying that [Nassif] was responsible for it”. He said Nassif had previously “left a message on my mobile that he was going to get me” in 2019.

“He didn’t speak English very well, so the threatening message probably went in one ear and out the other,” said Elliott. He said he had rejected two public attempts by Nassif to talk to him about developments.

Asked if Charles Perrottet was the “muscle” behind the scenes during the Perrottet government, Elliott said conservative right faction members would often say to him “I’ve got to check with Charlie”. Charles Perrottet, who has previously denied any wrongdoing, is the younger brother of former Liberal premier Dominic Perrottet, who has not been named in Icac’s allegations.

Elliott said he was aware of “speculation that Charles Perrottet and Jean Nassif were engaged in some way”.

Nassif, who fled Australia for rural Lebanon in 2022 after an investigation found dozens of defects in three separate residential developments constructed by the company, has previously denied any wrongdoing.

Elliott, who arrived at the inquiry on Friday telling Channel Nine “justice will prevail”, told reporters after giving evidence he planned to pursue his own legal action.

“And I must say also that it feels weird to be the first Liberal to ever be very happy to appear before Icac,” he said.

‘Loss of confidence’ in Catholic schools boss

In a statement shared on Friday, Catholic Schools NSW said its board had “unanimously determined that there is a loss of confidence in Dallas McInerney’s ability to lead the organisation into the future”.

“As such, the Board has now terminated Mr McInerney’s employment agreement with Catholic Schools NSW,” it said.

McInerney, whose Liberal party membership was suspended after the announcement of Icac’s inquiry, has insisted payments totalling $265,900 over four years to companies controlled by the Reformers were for genuine consulting work. On Wednesday, McInerney denied he performed a factory reset on a work phone and iPad over the weekend to wipe critical evidence.

McInerney, who is a factional ally of the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, has rejected that a message about a plan to “shake down Angus” referred to donations to the Reformers. Taylor is not named in Icac’s allegations and has repeatedly denied making payments to the Reformers.

In a statement provided to the Sydney Morning Herald on Friday, McInerney said: “When the inquiry started I said I would privilege the position of the company before my own. That is why I stood aside.

“I note the inquiry continues its important work and we are months away from findings and conclusions. I will forever remain grateful for the opportunity to serve, and hope I have made some positive contributions along the way.”

The interim CEO, Peter Yates, will remain in the role while a search process is conducted. The schools governing body said it would not make any statement about the inquiry or witnesses during public hearings, but said the allegations were of “deep concern” and it supported an “an externally conducted review of CSNSW’s operations”.

McInerney previously stood aside from his role as CEO of the governing body for 600 schools in NSW before the Icac hearings began “to allow the work of Catholic Schools NSW to continue its important mission”, he said in a statement. He was appointed as the inaugural CEO of the organisation in 2017.

On the inquiry’s first day, counsel assisting, Dr Peggy Dwyer SC, said it was not suggested that the schools governing body or its board were aware of the alleged actions by McInerney.

On Friday, Icac announced its witness list for next week, including Charles Perrottet and his wife, Anita Perrottet.

The inquiry continues.

With additional reporting by Jack Larkin.

australia.title: Alleged victim looked ‘distraught’ while sitting next to Alan Jones during restaurant luncheon, court hears
australia.snippet: Witness tells court veteran radio host’s hand was under table and that complainant C later looked ‘very upset’ Get our breaking news emai...
australia.content:
An alleged victim looked “distraught” while sitting next to Alan Jones, who had his hand under the table, a fellow guest at a lower north shore luncheon has told a Sydney court.

The alleged victim, known as complainant C, earlier told the court that Jones had instructed him to sit next to him at the long table and spent the entire lunch with his left hand under the table and either on his leg or on his penis over his pants.

Jones has pleaded not guilty to 20 charges of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching against six complainants.

On Friday the fellow guest told the court he could not see what was happening under the table but from his seat he did observe Jones spinning his wine in a glass in his right hand while his left hand was under the table.

“He looked distraught,” the guest said of C in Downing Centre local court.

His attention had been drawn to the alleged victim because two other guests closer to Jones and C appeared to be “startled” and “amused”, he said.

“As I was sitting this way out of the corner of my eye … people were laughing … Alan was spinning his wine and his left hand was under the table,” the first witness for C told the court. “They were startled, amused in a way.”

The lunch guest said when they left the restaurant, the two men were on the verge outside “ribbing” C about what allegedly happened.

“[They] were ribbing [C] about Alan’s hand and [one of them] said ‘you were copping a feel’.

“[C] was shaking his head saying ‘unbelievable,’” the witness told the court.

“His head was down. He didn’t look up. I distinctly remember thinking ‘something bad has happened here’.”

The witness said as they walked back to the car after lunch Jones was patting C on the back and squeezing him on the back of the neck.

“He looked very, very, very upset” and “absolutely devastated”, the witness said.

“He kind of reared away from the touch.”

The alleged victim earlier told the court he felt “deeply, deeply embarrassed”

when he realised a fellow guest was looking at him “while Alan was touching my penis”.

Prosecutor Georgina Wright asked if the fellow guest had a look on his face.

C replied: “Yes, it was a smirk.

“I didn’t want them thinking I was Alan’s toy. I know that sounds like a simplistic way of putting it, but they all made jokes about Alan being interested in young men.”

Defence counsel Michael Burke asked the witness why he didn’t mention the lower north shore restaurant incident in his interview with the journalist investigating Jones, the Sydney Morning Herald reporter Kate McClymont.

Burke suggested that if the incident had occurred he would have told McClymont.

Burke: “Your version of [what happened at the restaurant] is false.”

The witness: “No, it is all true.”

Burke: “You have reconstructed that version over time, haven’t you?”

The witness: “No.”

The trial before judge Glenn Walsh continues.

world.title: US deports 20 people to Liberia, the first of 1,200 migrants under Trump deal
world.snippet: Agreement is among largest third-country deportations driven by Trump administration’s immigration crackdown Twenty deportees from the Un...
world.content:
Twenty deportees from the United States arrived in Liberia on Thursday, as part of a new agreement that will see the west African country receive as many as 1,200 people under the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

The group arrived at the Roberts international airport outside the capital, Monrovia. The Liberia-US agreement is one of the largest third-country deportation arrangements pursued by the administration since Trump returned to office last year.

The Liberian information minister, Jerolinmek Piah said the 1,200 deportees will include African nationals as well as nationals from North America, South America and the Caribbean.

During a briefing on Tuesday, Liberia’s justice minister, Natu Oswald Tweh, said that the majority of the deportees had committed migration-related violations and offenses, and that they could seek asylum in the west African country if they wished.

The US has agreed to extend visitor visas for Liberians from 12 to 36 months and pledged $124m in assistance as part of the arrangement.

Under a series of often-secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to nearly two dozen countries that are not their own, advocates say, with about 10 of them in Africa. A new report by Refugees International and Human Rights First say the Trump administration has reached deals with at least 35 countries and has sent roughly 23,000 people to 26 of them as of early August, and makes the Liberia agreement the largest single arrangement so far.

Immigration lawyers have said the Trump administration uses deportations to third countries as a legal loophole to indirectly force asylum seekers back to their home countries.

In many cases, migrants are deported to countries they have never been to or where they face safety risks and are left with little choice other than to return to the home countries they were fleeing from.

A February report by Senate foreign relations committee Democrats found the Trump administration had paid more than $32m to five governments, several with poor human rights records, to accept about 300 third-country deportees – including $1.1m per person to Rwanda for seven deportees, and $7.5m to Equatorial Guinea for 29, a sum exceeding all US aid to that country over the previous eight years.

The report found more than 80% of those sent to third countries had since returned home anyway, often at further cost to taxpayers, and cited cases where deportees with US court-ordered protections were removed to Ghana and Equatorial Guinea before being sent onward within days.

The state department disputed the report’s characterization of its enforcement record.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

world.title: More than 100 dead after goldmine collapses in Central African Republic
world.snippet: The collapse was caused by a landslide, while local officials say the death toll is likely to rise as recovery efforts continue More than...
world.content:
More than 100 people have died after an artisanal goldmine at a small village in western Central African Republic (CAR) caved in due to a landslide, local officials and aid workers said on Wednesday.

The landslide happened on Tuesday afternoon in the village of Zamboye, about 50km (31 miles) from the town of Baboua and close to the border of Cameroon. Footage on social media appeared to show an avalanche of sand descend on a group of people, likely the miners, and cover them.

A statement by a local public prosecutor said many others were trapped under the deluge. It did not mention the number of fatalities. However, Gervais Ganagoroh, a Red Cross volunteer involved in the relief effort, told the Associated Press news agency on Wednesday that more than 100 bodies had been recovered from the collapse and ⁠a senior official at a local mining association confirmed that number to Reuters.

Local media in CAR reported that authorities had launched an investigation into the incident. A second prosecutor from Baboua told the press that the incident is believed to have been caused by “the collapse of several underground tunnels in which miners were operating”.

“The ground completely collapsed and buried people,” Cedric Mbango, a miner at the site, told the AFP news agency, describing the incident as “catastrophic”.

Rescuers are racing to retrieve the bodies of victims and find survivors among the miners, believed to be nationals of CAR and Cameroon. Authorities in Cameroon’s Eastern region said at least three of its citizens have been identified as victims in the incident.

Grégoire Mvongo, the region’s governor told state-owned radio on Wednesday that he was “working in close collaboration with our Central African colleagues to deal with the aftermath of this tragedy”.

Bertrand Be Yangué, a member of the Zamboye youth council, said that “finding them alive would be a miracle.” He added: “We are saddened and heartbroken to see young men and women perish after coming to the mines to save their families from despair.”

The toll is expected to rise as the rescue efforts continue, added Yangué.

The Central African news website Corbeau News reported that heavy machinery, including tractors, was being used in the retrieval mission and could jeopardise the rescue of those still alive under the landmass.

The exact number of people who were in the mine at the time of the cave-in remains unknown.

Small scale artisanal mines are common in different parts of Africa, despite regulations criminalising them, as unemployment continues to drive able-bodied men to abandoned or unused mines, to eke a living. The mining sites often operate with weak safety standards leading to repeated incidents: at least 40 people have died in several mining incidents in CAR this year alone.

world.title: Five Americans among seven killed in safari helicopter crash in Kenya
world.snippet: Officials say all seven people onboard killed, including Telemundo executive and Ecuador intelligence chief Seven people, including five ...
world.content:
Seven people, including five Americans, were killed when a safari helicopter crashed on Wednesday morning in a remote part of northern Kenya, according to local police and the state department.

Among the dead were an executive with Telemundo, the US-based Spanish-language network owned by NBC Universal, and the director of Ecuador’s national intelligence service.

The helicopter crashed at 9.13am while flying from the Loisaba Conservancy to the Ewaso Nyiro area in Samburu county, according to the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority, which said in a statement that an investigation was under way. It said there were seven people onboard – six passengers and the pilot.

Late on Wednesday, David Nkoroi, the police commander for Samburu, told reporters that all seven people onboard had died.

In Washington, the state department said five of those killed were US citizens. “The US embassy is in touch with local authorities and is providing consular assistance,” it said. “We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones on their loss.”

The identities of the victims were not revealed but a local television station in Miami, Florida, said that José Suárez, 55, president and GM of several Telemundo stations in Florida, was among those killed.

“We are heartbroken to learn the tragic news that José was killed in a helicopter accident in Kenya,” the NBC affiliate in Miami quoted from a joint statement from NBC Universal and Telemundo leadership.

The helicopter crashed in a rugged area in the foothills of Mount Ololokwe, a popular tourist destination in the country, local media reported. The helicopter, owned by local company Lady Lori Helicopters, was carrying guests with the travel company +Beyond.

Lady Lori Helicopters said in a statement that the aircraft was operating a charter flight when it crashed.

Tropic Air Kenya, a local safari operator, said in a statement that it dispatched two of its helicopters to aid search and rescue operations.

The aviation authority said the aircraft was a Eurocopter EC130 B4.

Ecuador confirmed later on Wednesday that Michele Sensi-Contugi, director of the country’s national intelligence center, died in the helicopter crash in Kenya.

In a statement posted on X, the presidency said: “In this moment of deep sorrow, the government extends its heartfelt condolences to his family, loved ones and close associates.”

Sensi-Contugi was visiting Kenya as a tourist with his wife, Stephany Hollihan Vasconez, who also died in the crash. She was a US and Ecuadorian citizen. They are survived by their two children.

Helicopter crashes have happened with increasing regularity in Kenya, which has a thriving tourism industry that depends on domestic carriers to ferry visitors to distant places like Mount Ololokwe.

In February, a legislator was among six people who died after a helicopter crash in a hilly area of western Kenya.

world.title: Spain to allow 500 children in Ceuta to go to mainland in immigration U-turn
world.snippet: Madrid government changes stance after previously saying anyone who entered territory illegally would be sent back Europe live – latest u...
world.content:
The Spanish government has U-turned and said it will allow 500 migrant children in Ceuta to relocate to the mainland.

The majority of the estimated 70,000 people who crossed into Ceuta – a Spanish territory on the coast of north Africa – on 30 July have returned to Morocco. However, under Spanish law, the state has a duty of care to young, unaccompanied migrants until they reach the age of 18.

On 13 August, the interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, had said: “Anyone who illegally enters Ceuta or Melilla [another Spanish enclave in north Africa] knows they will be sent back because Spain and Morocco work together to this end. They will not reach the peninsula, nor the European continent and nor will they remain indefinitely in Ceuta or Melilla.”

The transfer of the children to the Spanish mainland is a sensitive political topic as several regions governed jointly by the conservative People’s party and the far-right Vox are reluctant or opposed to receiving their quota.

To minimise conflict, the youth ministry, in coordination with the Ceuta government, is devising an urgent plan under which NGOs and child protection agencies take charge of the most vulnerable children, girls in particular, without transferring their guardianship to Spain’s regional governments.

Rubén Pérez Correa, the secretary of state for children, has been in Ceuta since Sunday in an effort to resolve a situation in which hundreds of children are living on the street and existing on handouts from Ceuta residents.

News of the government’s plan came only hours after the European Commission said that under EU law all of the migrants should be returned to Morocco. Asked to clarify, the commission’s spokesperson on internal affairs, Markus Lammert, said that by law all irregular migrants remaining in Ceuta should be sent back, “including unaccompanied minors”.

The People’s party has rejected the government plan, saying the best place for the children is with their families. “If Morocco has asked for the children to be returned and if Europe says the illegal immigrants should all be returned, whether children or not, what more does the government need?” the People’s party deputy finance spokesperson, Juan Bravo, said in a television interview.

The mixed messages partly derive from the fact the latest European pact on immigration has not yet been incorporated into Spanish law and therefore Spain’s own legislation on the treatment of unaccompanied minors remains in force.

According to Spain’s ministry of inclusion and migration, as of last March 21,104 people aged 16-23 were under guardianship of the state, of whom about 3,500 were under 17. Approximately 50% were from Morocco. Girls made up about 8% of the total.

world.title: Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo now deadliest in country’s history
world.snippet: At least 2,325 people have died from the virus, according to official data, with outbreak on track to be biggest in history The Ebola out...
world.content:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is now the deadliest in the country’s history, with at least 2,325 people dead, according to government data, surpassing the toll from the 2018-20 outbreak.

The DRC’s public health institute said confirmed cases had risen to 4,945, including 101 detected in the previous 24 hours.

The World Health Organization has said the outbreak is on track to surpass west Africa’s 2014-16 Ebola outbreak as the biggest in history. The 2014-16 outbreak resulted in 28,616 cases and 11,325 deaths across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, according to WHO data.

On Friday, the UN said Ebola “is winning in the Democratic Republic of the Congo” and said the epidemic was killing one person every 30 minutes.

Six of DRC’s 26 provinces have been affected, mainly those along the country’s north-eastern border. More than 3,400 of the cases have been recorded in Ituri province, where the outbreak was first reported.

The latest numbers of confirmed cases of Ebola in the DRC have made this outbreak – the 17th in the country’s history – the fastest-growing in the known history of the virus. It took almost five months for the 2014-16 west Africa outbreak to reach 1,000 deaths, compared with more than 2,000 deaths in less than three months in this outbreak.

There are no approved vaccines or treatments yet for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus that is responsible for the current surge in cases. Nonetheless, 1,000 people in the DRC have recovered from the infection, with 730 still in healthcare or isolation facilities.

Clinical trials of two possible treatments for the strain began last month in Ituri. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO director general, said last week that two vaccines developed specifically for Bundibugyo were now being tested on people.

Thomas Parisch, a public health specialist recently deployed to the DRC with Médecins Sans Frontières, said: “Normally, as an outbreak progresses, the case fatality ratio should fall as contact tracing improves and patients are identified and treated earlier. Instead, we’re still seeing many cases detected very late, when treatment is less likely to succeed, with many identified only after they die in the community.”

Uganda has reported at least 20 cases, all in the capital, Kampala. The last case reported there was on 21 June and no community transmission has been recorded. The government declared the country Ebola-free on 28 July after the last Ebola patient, a Congolese national, was discharged on 16 July.

In May, the WHO declared the outbreak in the DRC and Uganda as a public health emergency of international concern. It said sequencing showed the outbreak had started months earlier, in February.

Ebola is transmitted to people from wild animals and then spreads in the human population through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other body fluids of infected people, including dead bodies, and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding or clothing.

According to the WHO, symptoms can include fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle pain, headache and sore throat. These are followed by vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash and symptoms of impaired kidney and liver functions.

The response to this outbreak has been hampered by attacks on healthcare facilities, often fuelled by misinformation about safe burial practices, as well as strikes by some unpaid health workers. Decades of unrest and outside interference on traumatised communities, as well as poor health and road infrastructure have also complicated the picture.

More than 70% of people die in the community and not in health centres, said Mohamed Janabi, the WHO’s regional Africa director.

Jean-Paul Malo Lotsima, a civil society official in the Djugu area of Ituri, told the AFP news agency: “People prefer to be treated at home, thinking it is a case of poisoning or some other illness.”

He added: “It’s often at the last minute, when the family realises that the situation is getting worse, that patients are taken to hospital. And sometimes, they die on the way.”

Flavier Ngurima, who lives in Nizi, one of the hotspots of the outbreak in Ituri, said his brother died before reaching the treatment centre. “We had called on a nurse from the family to treat him at home because the patient and the family members were afraid to go to the ETC [treatment centre],” he said. “They said that over there, a lot of people die.”
